He remembers riding in the truck with his father between fields, listening to financial radio programs on the way. His parents gave generously of their time to their church, the steady unremarkable faithfulness of people who showed up because they believed it mattered. By the time he was teaching these principles to clients, he had believed them for years. But there is a difference, he told someone on our team, between believing something intellectually and having it reach your heart. He knew, theologically, that God owned it all. What took longer to land was what that meant for an ordinary week. Not just the giving line on the budget. Every line. The grocery run. The car payment. The amount saved and the amount spent without thinking. If God owns everything, then every decision about those resources is a stewardship decision, which makes it a spiritual one. Ron Blue says every spending decision is a spiritual decision, he explained. We tend to think of stewardship as only what we give. But if God owns everything, you are a steward of everything. A man reaps what he sows." **The Force That Never Stops Working** Early in my counseling career I kept a list I have referred to many times since, of people who earned extraordinary sums of money and still ended up with nothing. And alongside it I have carried the memory of people who never earned very much at all and ended their lives with genuine stability and enough to give away. The difference between those two groups was almost never the size of the income. It was the direction in which time was working for them, and whether they understood that time in a financial life is never neutral. It is always doing something. It is either quietly building you up or quietly wearing you down, and the mechanism in both cases is the same. Small amounts, repeated consistently, accumulate into something large. That is the whole of it. The only question is whether the accumulation is happening in your favor or against you. Scripture states the principle without any of the financial vocabulary we use for it today. Whoever gathers money little by little makes it grow. Notice the phrase: little by little. Not in one dramatic windfall, not through a clever shortcut, but through the patient repetition of small faithful additions over a long stretch of time. (Week 3)** **Day 16 — Start With Reality: You Can't Plan What You Won't Face** YOU CANNOT PLAN WHAT YOU WILL NOT FACE, AND THE TRUTH, ONCE YOU LOOK AT IT, IS ALMOST ALWAYS LESS FRIGHTENING THAN THE AVOIDING WAS. **John 8:32 (NIV):** "Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." **Psalm 139:23-24 (NIV):** "Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting." **The Number He Would Not Look At** An advisor connected to our work says the most common thing he encounters in a first meeting is not a bad set of numbers. It is a person who is afraid to look at the numbers they have. They arrive with a vague, heavy sense that something is wrong, a dread they have been carrying for months or years, and yet they have never actually sat down and written out what they earn, what they spend, and what they owe. The dread is real. The clarity is missing. And he has learned that the dread is almost always worse than whatever the clarity finally reveals, because a fear you refuse to name has no edges. It can be any size your imagination makes it. I have watched the same thing across nearly five decades of counseling. People will do almost anything rather than face the actual condition of their finances. They will work harder, worry more, move money around, and change the subject, all to avoid the one thing that would actually help, which is simply looking honestly at where they stand. And I understand the impulse, because looking feels like it might confirm the worst. But the opposite is usually true. The avoided problem grows in the dark. The named problem can finally be worked on. This week is the beginning of the planning section of our journey, and it has to begin exactly here, because you cannot build a plan on top of a reality you have refused to examine. **The Truth You Won't Face Controls You From the Dark** Jesus said

He would learn something in the material and then encounter it hours later at church or in his practice. And the truth that held him steadiest through the loss was the one that had first drawn him in. God owns it all, and he is in control of everything. Coming out of college, he was headed toward a conventional path in banking or financial advising, until the books he was reading, many of them Ron's and Larry Burkett's, pointed him somewhere else entirely. He went to work in a nonprofit financial ministry instead, and he has spent his career there, speaking in churches most weekends of the year about stewardship. The model his ministry runs is simple and quietly brilliant. People open savings accounts, retirement accounts, and giving funds with the ministry, earning a fair return on their money, and that pooled capital becomes loans to churches for building and expansion projects. Over the years, it has helped fund more than a thousand of them. He will tell you that this is far more exciting to him than helping build up someone's net worth for its own sake. He described one church in the Atlanta area that had financed its first building, then looked at a piece of unused land and asked how it could be a better steward of it. What they built was a set of small homes and a secure environment to rescue women out of trafficking and walk them through a multi-year path toward recovery. **THE GENEROSITY QUESTION · Why Does Giving Change Everything? (Week 4)** **Day 27 — Give First, and Give on Purpose: Discerning When and Where** GENEROSITY UNDER PRESSURE IS NOT GENEROSITY. REAL GIVING IS DECIDED AHEAD OF TIME, IN THE HEART, AND ON PURPOSE. **2 Corinthians 9:7 (NIV):** "Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." **Proverbs 3:27 (NIV):** "Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to act." **The Question I Learned to Ask Instead** For decades, when I sat with people who were wrestling with money and generosity, I found that challenging their giving directly almost never worked. If I told someone they should give more, I could produce guilt, but guilt is a terrible engine for generosity, and it never lasted. So I learned to ask a different set of questions entirely. What excites you? What are you passionate about? When you think about that next thing you want, why do you want it? I was not trying to talk anyone out of anything. I was trying to help them see their own heart more clearly, because the heart is where generosity actually begins. And then, gently, I would help them turn the question around. Instead of asking what do I want, what if the question became what could I give to? I have seen that single reframe change people, because it takes the same energy that was flowing toward acquiring the next thing and quietly redirects it toward a purpose larger than themselves. I have counseled many people who wanted things they did not really need and in some cases could not truly afford, and the wanting had a grip on them. But when they began asking what they could give toward instead, something shifted. **Welcome** Dear friend, I am glad you are here. For nearly fifty years I have sat across from people at every income level, from those wondering how to make it to the end of the month to those managing more than they ever imagined they would have, and I have watched the same thing again and again. The people who find real peace with money are almost never the ones who simply have the most of it. They are the ones who have settled a deeper question underneath the numbers, a question most of us were never taught to ask. Over the next thirty days, I want to walk that question with you, along with five others that grow out of it. We will start where everything has to start, with the question of who really owns it all, because until that one is settled, every other financial decision carries a weight it was never meant to carry. From there we will ask what the Bible actually says about money, and find that it offers a handful of ancient, reliable habits rather than the endless supply of clever shortcuts the world keeps selling. We will ask how a person finds true financial freedom, and discover that it was never a number to reach but a trust to settle. We will ask where to start, and do the honest, practical work of facing reality and building a plan you can actually keep. We will ask what God is growing through your financial life, and why. And we will finish with the question that quietly changes everything, why giving changes the giver even more than it changes anyone else. I want to be clear about what this is and what it is not. This is not a budgeting program, though there is real practical work ahead. It is a discipleship journey that happens to run straight through your checkbook. I have come to believe that money is one of the primary tools God uses to shape a human heart, not because accumulation is the point of life, but because what we do with our resources reveals, more honestly than almost anything else, what we actually trust. # WEEK TWO ## SESSION 2 · A: Assets Under Management ### Seeing how everything works together # Day 6 ## How Everything Works Together as a System ### From a collection of parts to a coordinated whole *Watch the Day 6 video before you read.* **"Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ."** 1 Corinthians 12:12 When you think about assets under management, what are you really helping a family understand? You're helping them to understand how everything works together as a system. Most families have assets spread among different places, sometimes with different advisors managing their money, different strategies, different structures. So the goal is to move from a collection of parts to a coordinated whole. I want to sit on the phrase collection of parts, because it describes almost every substantial family I have ever met and none of them would use it about themselves. They did not assemble a collection on purpose. A position got taken in one decade. An entity got formed because a transaction required it. An advisor got added because somebody made an introduction at the right moment. Every one of those decisions was defensible when it was made, by a competent person, for a real reason. Twenty years later the family owns a collection rather than a plan, and there was never a day when the collection was chosen. That is what makes it hard to see. Nothing went wrong. Things simply accumulated. Once you bring it all together, people begin to see differently. You can align strategies with goals, simplify where needed, and clarify how each piece fits into the overall plan. And that changes how decisions are made going forward. Instead of reacting to individual opportunities, you begin evaluating everything in the context of the whole. If you are the technical one, you can build something elegant and hand it to people who will tear each other apart over it. So you do not just want to know where the family is relationally, how they are doing over on that side. --- name: lifetogether-campaign-builder description: Build LifeTogether-style churchwide campaign content — 6-week/6-session campaign titles, weekly theme titles, session outlines, devotional themes, and brochure copy. Never propose more or fewer weeks unless the user explicitly asks for a different length. - Every campaign needs, in this order: one Title, one Subtitle/tagline, then 6 Weekly Themes (one per week). ## Title & Weekly Theme Pattern - **Churchwide flagship campaigns** (the main churchwide series — the "big six" style campaigns like "A Life That Matters," "Rooted," "Living Fully Alive"): use a repeating word or phrase device across all 6 weekly themes. - Example pattern: "Rooted in Christ / Rooted in Scripture / Rooted in Community / Rooted in Character / Rooted in Mission / Rooted for the Future." - This repeating device is a signature move for flagship campaigns — don't drop it. - **Specialized / niche editions** (life-stage editions, audience-specific spinoffs, one-off client campaigns): themes can vary in structure and wording. --- name: warm-pastoral-voice description: Applies Josh's warm, pastoral, invitational brand voice to curriculum, book, and website copy — the repeating-word device across parallel items (weekly themes, triads), the title+subtitle formula, and the "name the tension, resolve fast" pattern. Use this whenever drafting or editing titles, subtitles, weekly/session themes, brochure copy, chapter openers, taglines, or any client-facing text — even if the user doesn't say "voice" or "tone" explicitly. Trigger on requests like "give me themes for X," "draft a title for Y," "write brochure copy," or "make this sound like us." --- # Warm Pastoral Voice Josh's voice for churchwide curriculum, books, and website copy. Warm, pastoral, invitational. Never preachy, never academic. ## Core feel Every line should sound like an invitation, not an assignment. Short. Plain words. Forward-moving. If a sentence needs a semicolon or a subordinate clause to land, it's not this voice yet — break it apart. ## The repeating-word device This is the signature move. When listing parallel items (weekly themes, a triad of taglines, a list of "best for" audiences), lock every item into the *same grammatical scaffold* so the list reads like one sentence in six beats. **Pattern A — past participle + infinitive:** > Created to Know God / Designed to Belong / Formed to Become Like Jesus / Gifted to Serve / Sent to Make a Difference / Called to Multiply **Pattern B — imperative verb + "Your" + noun:** > Remember Your Story / Recognize Your Design / Renew Your Relationship / Refocus Your Season / Respond to Your Assignment / Reproduce Your Wisdom **Pattern C — anaphora triad (for taglines, 3 lines max):** > Helping Churches Go Deeper. / Helping Disciples Grow Stronger. / Helping Every Person Discover a Life That Matters. (Same opening word, widening scope each line: institution → group → individual.) Rule: pick ONE scaffold per list and hold it for every item. Don't let item 4 break the grammar of items 1

Generation here runs a few cents per document, not dollars. 3 Add the key to Netlify In your Netlify site: Site configuration → Environment variables → Add a variable . Key: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY . Value: the key you just created. Leave the scope on all deploy contexts. 4 Redeploy Functions read environment variables at deploy time, so the key needs one redeploy to take effect. # Auric Record **A movement of patient gold on deep ground.** Auric Record treats the picture plane as an instrument of quiet documentation. Its ground is always deep — a navy so dark it approaches the condition of night — and upon that ground it permits only two voices: fine gold line and whispered ivory text. Meaning is never illustrated; it is accumulated. A single mark says little, but hundreds of near-identical marks, laid down with monastic patience, become a ledger of time itself. The viewer should sense that every stroke was placed by a hand at the absolute top of its field, that the surface was labored over for countless hours, and that nothing — not one interval, not one weight — arrived by accident. Space in this movement is generous to the point of reverence. Compositions breathe asymmetrically: the recorded field gathers off-center, dense with concentric repetition, while vast passages of dark ground are left untouched so the accumulation can be felt as an event rather than a decoration. Scale contrast is the engine of drama — one great gathering of marks, one small one, and the long silent distance between them. The eye is asked to travel that distance and to understand it as the true subject. Color is a discipline, not a palette. The gold is calibrated like an instrument: most lines burn low, a few burn bright, and a single continuous stroke may be permitted full brilliance so that the eye can follow it the way a reader follows a sentence. Ivory appears only where language is essential, and even then it behaves as a material — letterspaced, measured, engraved rather than typeset. Texture is nearly subliminal: the faint tooth of paper, the barely perceptible tremor in a drawn circle that proves a hand, not a machine, kept the line alive. Rhythm comes from systematic observation. # Day 6 ## Not Technical, They're Relational and Emotional ### There are a few consistent barriers **"Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to your neighbor, for we are all members of one body."** Ephesians 4:25 There are a few consistent barriers, and most of them are not technical. They are relational and emotional. I want you to notice how much that sentence rules out. Not one of the reasons a family fails to have this conversation is a reason you were trained to address. There is no barrier here that a better structure removes. There is no barrier that a clearer illustration removes. You can build the finest plan of your career and every one of these will still be sitting in the room. The first is discomfort. These conversations touch money, expectations, roles, and sometimes deeper things like trust or past experience. People do not always know how to bring those up in a healthy way, so they avoid them. Read that carefully, because the mechanism is not what most people assume. It is not that the family does not want to talk. It is that nobody has a usable opening line. A sixty-five year old man who wants to tell his children how he thinks about the business does not lack the desire. He lacks a way to start that does not sound like an announcement, a summons, or a diagnosis, and so he waits for a natural opportunity that is never going to occur naturally. I have come to think of this as the most solvable barrier in the set, and the most consistently unaddressed. You can hand a family an opening. Almost nobody does. The second is fear. Fear of conflict, fear of being misunderstood, or fear of saying something that might create tension. So people stay quiet to keep things comfortable. If people do not feel safe, they will not engage. They may respond, but they will not really open up. I want you to hold those two verbs apart, because the whole session is in the gap between them. Responding is what a client does in a meeting where they have decided how much to give you. It is cooperative. It is polite. The answers are accurate as far as they go, and you will leave with a full page of notes. I have had two hour meetings where I got nothing but responses and did not notice until I tried to write the summary and found I could not say anything about that family I could not have said beforehand. Opening up is different, and it costs the person something. They are telling you a thing that could be used, and they are handing you a piece of information that changes how you see them. Nobody does the second one because you asked nicely. They do it because they have concluded it is safe. So the practical question is what a person is actually assessing when they make that call, and it is not your credentials. It is three things, and you can influence all three. The first is whether you will handle it well. Not whether you will agree. Whether the thing they say will be received without a flinch, a correction, or a look exchanged with someone else in the room. The second is whether it will stay where they put it. In a family setting this is enormous, because they are not only trusting you, they are calculating what you will repeat to their mother. The third is whether the meeting has room for it. This one is structural rather than personal, and it is the one advisors control most directly and think about least. You are talking about value, responsibility, fairness, and sometimes identity. That is why these particular topics create so much tension. They are personal. I have watched advisors miss this for entire careers, and the reason is straightforward. We are trained to treat money as a quantity, and as a quantity it behaves predictably. It can be divided, valued, projected, and compared. Everything in our professional apparatus assumes that a dollar is a dollar regardless of whose hand it is in. Inside a family, it is not. --- name: cover-designer description: Generate distinct, image-led cover art for curriculum, campaign, and product titles — image-model art direction (Nano Banana / Gemini), original code-built art, or treatment of a supplied image — where the image is built from the title's essence and series covers read as a family. Use whenever Brett supplies a title and subtitle and wants a cover, cover art, thumbnail, packaging, or a visual identity, or whenever a new title, series, or catalog exists without art. Never deliver type sitting on a plain colored background. --- # Cover Designer The title is the source. The image is its expression. The composition returns the eye to the words. ## Non-negotiables - **Image-led.** Full-bleed artwork occupies the entire canvas. A flat or gradient background with a font on it is a failed cover, no matter how nice the font. The bar is a unique, signature, top-designer piece — never something that reads as AI-templated. - **Derived from the title.** Extract the essence, heart, and theme of the title and subtitle, then choose one central visual metaphor unique to this title. The image is based on the words, not decorated near them. - **Directional.** The art's energy — light, converging lines, a lit zone — leads the eye to the title block. - **Distinct.** No two titles in a catalog share a metaphor. On catalog work, keep a running motif ledger and check it before designing each cover; at hundreds or thousands of titles this ledger is the only thing preventing repeats. - **The removal test.** Hide the words. What remains should still stand as a piece of art about the theme. ## Process 1. **Gather**: title, subtitle, series membership, format (default 2:3 portrait; square thumbnail crop on request), and lane. 2. **Essence brief** (3 lines, before any pixels or prompts): the heart of the title / its emotional register / the one central metaphor. # Worked Example — The "40 Days of ___" Family This is a reference build showing the full method: philosophy, family system, and three per-title essence briefs. New series get their own philosophy and system; reuse the shape of this document, not its contents. ## Design Philosophy — "Luminous Passage" Light is the protagonist. Every composition is a passage of light moving through a field of deep, saturated color — light that has somewhere to go and something to touch. The darkness is never empty; it is the depth that makes the light legible. The work should feel like a moment held still: the instant before dawn breaks, the second a seed leaves the hand, the breath a flame takes before it stands. Space is generous and vertical. One focal event commands the canvas; everything else is atmosphere serving it. Vast fields of color breathe around the event the way silence surrounds a single spoken word. Nothing crowds. Nothing decorates. Every mark that exists, exists because the composition needs it. Color works in deep grounds and one luminous counterpoint. The ground is rich and enveloping — indigo, garnet, storm teal — and the counterpoint is warm and alive: gold, ember, dawn. Surfaces carry the tooth of printed lithography: fine grain, soft vignette, ink that feels pressed into paper rather than lit on a screen. Rhythm comes from patient accumulation. Small repeated marks — rings, seeds, streaks — gather in the hundreds until repetition itself becomes meaning, the way daily practice becomes formation. The accumulation must look meticulously placed, the product of countless hours, rewarding a viewer who leans in. Composition converges. Light rays, particle paths, halos, and lit zones all conduct the eye to a single destination, and that destination is the word. Typography is not laid over the art; it is where the art arrives. Text stays minimal — an eyebrow, a title, a subtitle, a mark — set with painstaking, master-level care, every measurement the result of refineme

# GOD OWNS IT ALL — 40 DAYS ## Days 2–7: Rebuilt Drafts with Story Guidance --- > **HOW TO READ THE STORY CALLOUTS** > Each day that needs an additional story contains a clearly marked block: > **[STORY NEEDED — Source / Type / Placement / Tone]** > These are editorial flags for the production team. The story slot is already written into the devotional structure — it just needs the real testimony dropped in. The surrounding text will remain as written. --- # DAY 2 ## The Second Chair ### *Why Surrender Isn't Loss — It's Relief* --- *God doesn't ask you to carry everything. He asks you to trust him first.* --- **TODAY'S VERSES** *"Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight."* — Proverbs 3:5–6 (NIV) *"Casting all your cares on him, because he cares about you."* — 1 Peter 5:7 (CSB) --- Picture yourself at your boss's dinner table. He's invited a group of colleagues and you're determined to make a good impression. The meal is ready. Your boss steps out of the kitchen and moves toward the head of the table. Before he can sit down, you walk past him and take the seat yourself. Nobody does that. Not because of a rule, but because the arrangement is obvious. In your boss's home, at his table, the head chair is his. You wait to be seated because he is the host. That picture is what I mean by the second chair. In every life there is a first chair — the seat of ultimate authority. And the question isn't whether a first chair exists. It's who sits in it. If God sits there, you can live with steadiness. If you sit there, you may look capable on the outside while your soul quietly exhausts itself trying to hold everything together. I saw this play out for decades in my practice. I worked with CEOs, surgeons, pastors, single parents, and retired couples. Across all of them I noticed the same pattern: the people who lived with the most peace weren't the ones with the most money.

This mirrors the pedagogical arc Ron Blue has taught for decades. The framework earns its skeleton. What it lacks is internal momentum. Right now the outline reads like a table of contents for six separate studies rather than a unified 40-day transformation. Individual days are intellectually correct but emotionally inert. The reader can see the topics coming without feeling pulled forward. A truly cohesive devotional should feel like a river — you sense the current building — not like a collection of labeled ponds. The deeper problem: **the outline does not adequately reflect Ron Blue's core conviction that behavior follows belief**. The six movements are organized around questions and concepts, but the reader's lived experience — the fear, the grip, the restlessness, the comparison, the weight of carrying too much — doesn't pulse through enough. Concepts are introduced before the reader has been given permission to feel the weight they're already carrying. --- ### Section-by-Section Evaluation **SECTION I — THE OWNERSHIP QUESTION (Days 1–7)** Strong foundation. # DAY 1 # Not Just What You Leave Behind ## It's What You Pass On Every Day **"A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children."** PROVERBS 13:22 Most people think of legacy as something that happens later. I understood it that way for a long time, and I was trained in a profession that reinforces it at every turn. The documents get drafted for a moment none of us will be in the room for. The plan gets built around a date nobody can name. Everything about the way we work says this is a future event. Legacy is not just what you leave behind. It's what you pass on every day. Those are two different verbs and they operate on completely different terms. Leaving is a transaction. It happens once, it happens after you are gone, and it is administered by people you hired and paid. Passing on is not a transaction at all. It is happening right now, in how you live, what you prioritize, and how you relate to others. Nobody has been hired to handle it. There is no closing date and no signature page. Which changes the question. For most of my career the question in the room was some version of, what will I leave. The better question, and the one I put to families early now, is, what am I building into the lives around me. Here is the part that took me the longest to accept. Often, what gets passed on most clearly is not what was intended. It's what was lived. The intended legacy is the one in the documents. It is careful, it has been reviewed, and it usually reflects a person at his best. The lived legacy is what the children actually observed over thirty years, and it was never reviewed by anyone. No child in the history of this work has ever read the trust and concluded something about his father. He concluded it from watching his father. I want to be precise about the mechanism, because this is where advisors get it wrong. It is not that the lived legacy competes with the intended one and sometimes wins. It means there's enough shared understanding that people can move forward together. I want to spend the whole reading on that definition, because I have watched advisors set the wrong target for years and then conclude that alignment work does not succeed. The wrong target is agreement. It is an understandable mistake, because agreement is visible and it can be documented and it makes a meeting feel finished. It is also the wrong thing to pursue in a family, and the reason is arithmetic rather than philosophy. A son can understand exactly why his father intends to leave the bulk of the estate to charity, be able to state the reasoning accurately, and still wish it were otherwise. That family is aligned. They are operating from them right now, in how they spend, who they help, what they tolerate, and which grandchild gets called first when something goes wrong. None of that required a document. What most of them do not have is any articulated version of it. The values are running the family without ever having been said out loud, which works reasonably well until the family has to make a decision that the values would have settled and instead has to be argued. That is the actual mechanism. It is not that families lack values. It is that undeclared values cannot be used as a reference point, so every decision gets litigated on its own terms, and the results drift apart from each other over a decade until somebody notices the family has been going in two directions. Your role here is smaller and more useful than it sounds. You are not helping a family invent what matters to them. You are helping them find language for something that has been there the whole time. You are not trying to force a list. # SESSION 4 # Creating Alignment in the Family ## Getting Everyone on the Same Page ## INTRODUCTION > **KEY VERSE** > > "Do two walk together unless they have agreed to do so?" > > **AMOS 3:3** Clarity is an individual achievement. A man can be completely clear about what he wants and his wife can be completely clear about what she wants and the two can be incompatible, and nothing about the clarity of either position moves the family an inch. This is the gap that surprises advisors. You do good work in the values conversation, everyone leaves the room satisfied, and eighteen months later the family is stuck again on something that should have been settled. What happened is that five people each got clearer about their own position without any of them getting closer to each other. The word alignment gets used loosely in this profession, usually to mean agreement, and that is the wrong target. Families do not need to want the same things. They need enough shared understanding to move in the same direction while wanting somewhat different things, which is a much lower bar and a much more durable one. The thing that prevents alignment is almost never conflict. It is assumption, which is quieter and considerably more dangerous, because a family in conflict knows it has a problem. Alignment does not mean everyone thinks the same. It means there is enough shared understanding to move forward together. ## OPENING STORY ### They Thought They Had Said It The parents were certain. Everyone in the room knows what the subject is. Nobody raises it. The meeting proceeds efficiently through matters of much smaller consequence, and everyone leaves feeling that it went fine. Advisors learn to recognize that silence and then, very often, learn to work around it, because the alternative is to be the person who names it. The usual explanation for why these conversations fail is that families are conflict averse or poorly led or carrying old wounds, and sometimes all of that is true. Tom's explanation is different and more useful. Communication breaks down in these families not because people care too little but because the subject matters too much. When you are talking about values, expectations, roles, or the future, you are not exchanging information. You are exposing identity, and people protect that instinctively. Which means the failure is not a character problem. It is a design problem, and design problems have solutions. The honest human signal was the *later* sends: ~25% opens, **~1.7% clicks.** - A **deliverability crash** mid-campaign (Apr 15–16: 2.5% and 1.8% opens, a 23% bounce) followed a ~39k single-day blast — classic new-domain reputation damage. - **Over-mailing:** 7 sends in the final 8 days, including three "LAST CALL" emails in a row. Opens drifted down (26% → 19.9%); unsubscribes rose to ~0.29%. **The only metric bots can't fake is registrations. That number was 9.** --- ## 2. What 9 registrations actually means It rules things in and out: - **Not an email-craft problem.** You cannot subject-line your way from 9 to a full room. The copy was never the bottleneck. - **Not (mainly) a broken-page problem.** If most early clicks were bots, real human traffic to the page was small — so "lots of traffic, no conversion" isn't the story. - **It IS a re-engagement + offer-friction + targeting problem.** The audience is *right* — faith-based financial advisors are exactly Tom's people. But two things worked against us: 1. **They didn't know Tom.** Credibility was never established before the ask. 2. **The ask was huge and cold:** $2,500 + two days + travel, pitched directly to people who'd never heard of him. Cold-ish audience + unknown authority + high-friction offer = the hardest sell in marketing. 9 isn't a broken campaign; it's the predictable result of skipping the trust step. --- ## 3. Helping families focus on what matters most “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” Psalm 90:12, NIV When people think about legacy, the word tends to stay big and broad. It floats. Everyone agrees it matters, and almost no one can say what it is. Ask a successful couple what they want their legacy to be, and you will often get a long pause, because the question is too large to hold all at once. That is why Tom does not start with one question. He starts with five areas, and the first is the most personal of all. Your personal legacy. What do you want to be remembered for? And inside that question sits another one, quieter and deeper. What is your spiritual legacy going to be? From there the areas unfold. Your family legacy, the story your children and grandchildren are living in right now. Your financial legacy, the wealth transfer, and whether the inheritance you leave will be a blessing or a curse, because money left to unprepared hands does not benefit a life, it burdens one. Your business legacy, if you own one, and the honest questions of succession and continuity. And your charitable legacy, what you want to do for the Kingdom of God, both now and at the end of life. Five areas instead of one squishy word. That is the whole move. Clarity does not come from thinking harder about a vague idea. It comes from breaking the idea into places you can actually stand and look around. The Principle Legacy becomes clear when it becomes specific. A family cannot aim at “leaving a legacy,” but they can answer what they want to be remembered for, what they hope for their children, what their wealth should do, what happens to the business, and what they will give. # Launching Flourishing LifeTogether ### What Transfers from Purpose Driven, What's Actually Missing, and the Plan to Close the Gap --- ## Part One: Transferable Principles (Not Just Tactics) The nine mechanics from Part Two are tactics. Underneath them are five principles that transfer regardless of brand — these are what Flourishing LifeTogether should actually borrow, not the specific tools: 1. **Content follows commitment, not the reverse.** The book didn't summarize the church campaign — the campaign followed the book's momentum. Individual pull has to exist before institutional push works. 2. **Completeness beats brilliance.** A finished, mediocre kit gets used. A brilliant, half-finished framework gets admired and shelved. Nothing launches until the whole kit exists — sermon outlines, session content, family and kids editions, all of it. 3. **Doctrinal minimalism is a growth strategy, not a compromise.** The fewer specific theological commitments required, the wider the door. This is already true of the five-purposes foundation; the discipline is refusing to add anything more specific as it scales. 4. **Proximity-based coordination beats isolated asks.** A pastor says yes faster when twenty peers in the same city are already saying yes. Coalition-building is a recruitment mechanism, not a downstream outcome of success. 5. **Trust compounds from a small, credible base.** National reach is never the starting move — it's what happens after a handful of pilots produce results real enough to talk about without exaggeration. None of these require copying Purpose Driven's specific brand, book, or campaign structure. Encodes hard-won technical rules; never build a designed PDF from scratch without this skill. --- # Print PDF Producer ## Page discipline — author pages, don't flow them Author **one `.pg` div per sheet** and fill each deliberately. The container that works (do not improvise): ```css @page{size:8.5in 11in;margin:0} .pg{width:8.5in;height:11in;padding:0.72in 0.92in 1.15in;position:relative; overflow:hidden;display:block;page-break-after:always;break-after:page} .foot{position:absolute;left:.92in;right:.92in;bottom:.52in;border-top:1px solid /*line color*/} ``` **Never use flex for the page container** — flex + fixed height lets the body overflow and drags footers onto the next sheet, cascading. Screen-only `margin-bottom` on `.pg` is fine with `@media print{.pg{margin:0}}`. ## Verification loop — run every render 1. Count `.pg` divs in source; render; **assert PDF page count matches.** Mismatch = an overflowing page. 2. Rasterize at 50dpi (`pdftoppm -png -r 50`); per page, measure the gap from footer rule up to last inked row. Over ~0.85in of bottom whitespace → add copy (~250 characters of prose per inch at 11pt/1.62); page-count growth → cut copy. 3. Extract text per page with pypdf; a page under ~650 characters is a spillover orphan — tighten the source page above it. Remove any global `break-inside:avoid`. 4. Deliberately centered pages (covers, closers) get balanced top padding so the gap reads intentional. ## Design rules - **Every page gets a ground** — never black type on bare white sheets; run a color rhythm across the spread. - **Never introduce a color outside the client's palette** (an invented cream reads

It reads instructions. When the instruction is thin, the result is thin, and most people blame the tool when the real issue is the ask. Nearly every disappointing answer traces back to one of four gaps. 1 It lacks context The model is handed a task with none of the background a capable assistant would need to do it well. 2 It is vague Wishes stand in for specifics. # FAMILY CLARITY GUIDE — AUDIT Would a family actually go through this, and would it help them. Written against the guide as it now stands, after the case studies were replaced. --- # THE HEADLINE PROBLEM **185 questions across six sessions. About 31 per session.** An advisor can absorb that. Advisors consume professional development for a living, they read densely, and they are being paid to get better at this. A family sitting in a living room on a Tuesday will answer eight or nine. That is not a small gap. It means the guide is currently designed for a reader who does not exist, and the family will handle it the way people always handle an overloaded worksheet. They will do the easy questions and skip the hard ones. Which is backwards, because the hard ones are the product. **The guide also never says which questions matter most.** Reflect explicitly says "there are more here than you need, take the ones that catch," which is honest but is also the guide admitting it overshot. Nothing else in the session says that, so the reader is left assuming the other twenty-five are all required. **What I would do.** Mark one question in each session as the one that matters. Not a summary, a marked question. If a family answers only that one, the session worked. Everything else becomes optional by contrast rather than by omission. --- # WHAT THE GUIDE ASSUMES It assumes more than it should, and it assumes it silently. | Assumption | How often | Problem | | --- | --- | --- | | You are married | "your spouse" 37 times, "your marriage" 8 | Widowed, divorced, single, or married to someone who will not participate | | You have children | "your children" 21 | No children, estranged children, one child rather than several | | You have assets to transfer | throughout Session 4 | A family with modest resources is told the session is for them once, in the last line | | You share a faith | "God" 13 times, six Scripture passages, Going Deeper in every session | An adult child or in-law

Not as tone, as mechanism. Tom says it plainly on camera: - The facilitator exists so Dad is one voice among ten, not the person running the room. Mom and Dad get two votes out of ten. - The advisor advocates for the kids because "the kids would never say that to their parents, but you can say it. And you don't have a dog in the fight." - The advisor asks the question nobody in the family will ask. "You intimidate your kids." The wife confirms it. A family member cannot deliver that line. - Tom interviews the next generation separately, then reports back to Mom and Dad. Remove that person and roughly a third of the coaching content has no mechanism. This is the design problem. Vocabulary is the easy part. ## What the family edition has to answer that the coaching edition never asks **Who asks the hard question when there is no coach in the room?** Every Family title needs a working answer. It doesn't mean giving. **"As each one has received a special gift, employ it in serving one another as good stewards of the multifaceted grace of God."** 1 PETER 4:10 I am going to say something that sounds harsh about the church, and I say it as somebody who loves the church. The church has ruined the word stewardship. We have stewardship campaigns. We have stewardship Sundays. And because of that, an entire generation hears the word and thinks it means giving, specifically giving to the church, specifically right now. Look it up. Stewardship means management. It does not mean giving. Giving is one thing a steward does with what they manage, and it is not the whole job. Stewardship is managing everything you have been entrusted with. Your money. Your time. Your relationships. Your health. Your influence. All of it. I care about this distinction because of what it does to how families teach their children. If stewardship means giving, then teaching stewardship means teaching a child to put something in an envelope. That is good and it is one lesson. If stewardship means management, then teaching stewardship means teaching a child to handle what they have been given, which is a far larger curriculum and one that occupies years rather than an afternoon. Here is the practical consequence. Families who hold the narrow definition teach generosity and assume competence will develop on its own. It does not. Generosity without management produces people who give impulsively and cannot sustain it. And management without generosity produces something worse, which is competence in the service of accumulation. Peter says each has received a gift and should employ it as a good steward. # SESSION 4 ## Wealth and Wisdom *Why one without the other does not work* # Day 16 ## The Twin W's ### Every family passes on both **"Acquire wisdom; and with all your acquiring, get understanding."** PROVERBS 4:7 Every family passes on two things. Wealth and wisdom. We call them the twin W's, and the reason for the pairing is that they always travel together, whether or not anybody arranged it. The question is never whether both are being transferred. It is what condition each of them is in when it arrives. Here is the asymmetry that causes most of the trouble. Wealth transfers on its own. It has custodians, statements, documents, and a legal system built to move it. You could do nothing and it would still arrive, at a date determined by events rather than by you. Wisdom has no such machinery. There is no institution responsible for it. Nobody sends a reminder. It moves only if a person deliberately moves it, over years, and it moves through relationship rather than through paperwork. Which means the two are on completely different timelines and only one of them is on a schedule. And here is what follows. If a family does nothing in particular, wealth arrives fully and wisdom arrives partially or not at all, and the family will experience that as a surprise despite it being entirely predictable. Now, I want to define wisdom here, because it is a word that can float free. I do not primarily mean spiritual insight, though that is part of it. I mean the accumulated practical judgment that produced whatever your family has. How to make a decision under uncertainty. What a dollar costs to earn. How to tell whether somebody is trustworthy. When to hold and when to move. What matters and what only looks like it matters. That is a real body of knowledge and it exists almost entirely in your head. Proverbs says acquire wisdom, and with all your acquiring, get understanding. The construction is interesting. It assumes acquiring is happening. It is not counseling against it.

The Questions — Family Legacy by Design The Questions The Questions Families Actually Ask. Every advisor hears the same questions in the same order. All Questions Family Meetings Money & Numbers Giving Next Generation Hard Conversations Talking Points How To Open It, From Either Side. For The Advisor · Not Shown To Families Introducing This To A Client Family Four moves, in order. Say them in your own words — change anything that does not sound like you. “Before we talk about the plan, I want to ask about the family.” Signal the shift before making it. “Most families I sit with have a strong plan and a quiet table. I don’t want that for you.” Name the gap without naming their gap. “There’s a short assessment — ten minutes, the two of you, no numbers.” Make the first step small and specific. “Then I’d like to give your family a thirty-day journey. On me.” Gift it. Do not sell it. Drafts, not scripts. The point is the order, not the wording. For The Family Asking Your Advisor Or Pastor For This If your family wants to start and your advisor has not raised it, this is how to raise it yourself. “I read something that named what I’ve been worried about.” Start with the worry, not the product. “It’s not about the plan. It’s about whether our kids are ready for it.” Move the subject to the people. “There’s a ten-minute assessment. Would you walk through it with us?” Give them a role they can say yes to. “If this isn’t your lane, is there someone you’d point us to?” Leave a door open either way. Bring one printed reading to the meeting. It does more than a description. When A Short Answer Isn’t Enough Every Question Here Has A Course Behind It. --- name: pastoral-voice description: Applies LifeTogether's warm, pastoral, invitational voice to any campaign title, subtitle, tagline, weekly theme, brochure copy, devotional line, or sermon-series description. Use this whenever writing or revising copy for the Biblical Purpose Library, the Seven Day Experience, or any related LifeTogether material — even if the user just says "write a campaign" or "give me themes" without mentioning tone. Always run copy through these voice rules before presenting it; never let output drift academic, corporate, or preachy on this project. --- # Pastoral Voice A voice skill, not a content-structure skill. It governs *how things are said* — word choice, sentence rhythm, and emotional register — for LifeTogether copy. Pair it with the lifetogether-campaign-builder skill's title → subtitle → 6 themes → confirm → expand workflow; this skill shapes what fills each of those slots. ## The register: warm, pastoral, invitational Three failure modes to actively avoid: - **Preachy**: telling the reader what they must do or feel. ("You must surrender every area." / "Repent and change today.") Fix by inviting instead of commanding: swap the imperative-at-the-reader for an imperative-with-the-reader, or a question. - **Academic**: doctrinal terminology, footnote energy, explaining a concept instead of extending an invitation. ("This series explores the soteriological implications of...") Fix by naming the human experience first, theology second and lightly. - **Corporate**: hype and buzzwords borrowed from marketing decks. ("A revolutionary, game-changing framework to optimize your spiritual growth.") Fix by trusting plain words — the brand's whole appeal is that it doesn't sound like a pitch. The tell that copy has drifted into one of these: read it aloud. If it sounds like a memo, a lecture, or an ad, it's off. It should sound like a trusted pastor talking to one person over coffee. ## Sentence rhythm - **Taglines / section headers**: 3–6 wo

# Deploying 40daycampaigns.com to Netlify This site is static HTML plus two small serverless functions (a Claude proxy and a Stripe checkout creator). Netlify hosts both from this one folder. Nothing needs to be built first — the site ships ready. ## 1. Put the folder on Netlify Easiest: at app.netlify.com choose **Add new site → Deploy manually** and drag this entire folder (the one containing `index.html`, `netlify.toml`, and `netlify/`) onto the drop zone. Netlify reads `netlify.toml`, publishes the static files, and bundles the functions automatically. For ongoing edits, connect the folder to a Git repo instead and Netlify will redeploy on every push. Leave the build command empty and the publish directory as `.` — both are already set in `netlify.toml`. ## 2. Set four environment variables Site settings → **Environment variables** → Add: | Key | Value | Used by | |---|---|---| | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `sk-ant-…` (from console.anthropic.com) | Claude "Enhance" in the Builder | | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | `sk_live_…` (or `sk_test_…` to trial) | Card checkout | | `SITE_URL` | `https://YOURSITE.netlify.app` (or your domain) | Stripe success/cancel redirects | | `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` | same as SITE_URL (optional; locks the functions to your domain) | both functions | Redeploy once after setting them (Deploys → Trigger deploy) so the functions pick them up. ## 3. Point your domain (optional) Domain settings → add `40daycampaigns.com`. Netlify issues the HTTPS certificate automatically. Update `SITE_URL` to the custom domain afterward. ## 4. Stripe receipts (optional but recommended) Card payments already work after step 2. To record paid orders and send real receipts, create a webhook in the Stripe dashboard pointing at `https://YOURSITE/.netlify/functions/stripe-webhook` for the event `checkout.session.completed`, then add `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET = whsec_…` to your Netlify env vars. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ board_extract.py ================ Reconstruct board rosters across many nonprofits from IRS Form 990 / 990-PF data. Solves the problem that manual research cannot: ~25 organizations x ~10 years of filings x ~15 officers per filing = several thousand rows. This pulls them all, then derives (a) who is current, (b) who departed and when, and (c) which people sit on more than one board in your set. DATA SOURCE ----------- ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer API (free, public, no key required), which mirrors the IRS e-file XML release. Filings are the authoritative record: Part VII of the 990 and Part VIII of the 990-PF list every officer, director, and trustee. KNOWN LIMITS -- read these before trusting output ------------------------------------------------- 1. Organizations the IRS designates as churches or associations of churches file NOTHING. They will come back empty. That is a real finding, not a bug -- see CHURCH_STATUS_LIKELY below. For those, check the org's own website for a voluntary "public disclosure copy." 2. Only e-filed returns have XML. Paper filings before ~2018 may be image-only and will not parse. Coverage is strong 2018+, patchy before. 3. Filings lag 12-24 months. The most recent roster on file is not necessarily today's board. Always confirm current members against the org's own site. 4. Name matching for interlocks is fuzzy. "ROBERT H MACLELLAN" and "BOB MACLELLAN" will not match; "JOHN SMITH" at two orgs may be two people. Treat interlocks.csv as a lead list requiring human confirmation. 5. 990 Part VII mixes trustees with paid staff. Filter on the title column. USAGE ----- pip install requests python board_extract.py # uses ORGS below python board_extract.py --orgs my.txt # one org name (or EIN) per line python board_extract.py --out ./results OUTPUT ------ rosters_long.csv one row per person per filing year roster_summary.csv one row per person per org, with first/last year + status interlocks.csv people appearing at 2+ o

Each day escalates slightly on the one before. --- **DAY 1 · Give something you can hold.** Not money — an object you actually use. Money is abstract and easy; a thing you have to carry out to the car is not. Something in your house today belongs in someone else's. **DAY 2 · Give to someone who cannot repay you.** Jesus said to invite the people who can't return the favor. Most of our generosity quietly circulates among people who might one day be useful to us. Break that today. **DAY 3 · Give without anyone knowing.** No credit, no mention, no post. # QUIET GRAVITY ### A design philosophy for the Living Obedience covers --- **The movement.** Weight without noise. This is an aesthetic built for subjects too serious to shout about — where the drama lives in the density of the dark rather than the brightness of the light, and where a single warm source is asked to do the work that a lesser hand would give to ten. Everything is atmosphere. Nothing is illustration. **Space and form.** The canvas is a deep field, unbroken, that the eye must adjust to before it can see. Form arrives slowly: an edge, a horizon, a line — never an object. The composition holds a single structural event and refuses to add a second. Vast tracts of the surface do nothing at all, and that emptiness is the most laboured part of the work; it has been tuned across dozens of passes until the darkness itself has tonal variation, a quiet internal weather that rewards long looking and is invisible at a glance. The lower third is reserved and slightly settled, a place where light pools and the eye comes to rest. **Colour and material.** A palette of two temperatures in permanent negotiation — a cold, deep, ink-blue ground and a warm gold that never becomes yellow and never becomes orange. Between them sits a narrow band of indigo and umber where the two argue, and that band is where the piece actually lives. Colour is layered rather than applied: field over field over field, each one nearly transparent, accumulated with the patience of glaze on panel. Over everything, a fine analogue grain — the tooth of paper, the noise of film — so that the surface reads as a made thing rather than a rendered one, and a vignette so gentle that it is felt rather than seen. **Scale and rhythm.** One gesture, held large. The single luminous event occupies a commanding portion of the field and then stops; there is no secondary flourish, no supporting mark, no decoration in the corners. Irrational Obedience — The Elements A proposal from LifeTogether Irrational Obedience Saying yes to God before the reasons arrive — with your life, your family, your business, your wealth. Prepared for Dale Armstrong and the Board of The Signatry · August 2026 The board approved a book. What follows is that book — and the seven things that come out of it, with a specimen of each, so nobody has to imagine what is being commissioned. The investment is set out at the back. 01 Section one · the idea What Irrational Obedience is I am living. And I bend a knee to God the Father — so that everything I do from this point forward is His. Everything with my family. Everything with my work. Everything with my money. Not someday. Now. Every ask God makes in Scripture fails the reasonable test at the moment it is made. Build a boat with no rain. Send thirty-one thousand seven hundred soldiers home. Give back the son you waited a century for. Cook your last meal for a stranger. Irrational is the observer's word, never the obeyer's — and the book's whole job is to show what the person obeying could see that the person watching could not. Why obedience and not generosity Generosity is the outflow, not the entry point. A book about giving reaches people who already think of themselves as givers. A book about saying yes reaches everyone — and produces givers as a consequence. Why irrational Irrational generosity would concede that the giving makes no sense. Irrational obedience describes what the disciples actually did. Leaving the nets mid-workday is irrational by every worldly measure, and Scripture tells it approvingly. 05 Section five · the moment The pledge that changed philanthropy has a gap in it In 2010 Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates and Warren Buffett invited the wealthiest families in the world to commit at least half of their wealth to charity. Roughly two hundred and fifty families across some thirty countries have signed. Each one writes a letter explaining why. It is a moral commitment rather than a legal one, and it changed the conversation permanently. But fifteen years in, the honest reporting on it says two things. Most signatories are wealthier than when they signed. And the majority of the money that has moved has moved into private foundations and donor-advised funds rather than into the hands of the work. The world's most successful philanthropic pledge asks families what they will give eventually. Almost nobody has asked them what they will live now. What that leaves open A commitment measured at death rather than during life. A promise about a percentage rather than a pattern. A signature from one person rather than a decision made by a family. And a structure in which the generosity is real but the formation never happens. Why this house in particular The Signatry holds the infrastructure that the parked money already sits in — which means it is uniquely positioned to be the organisation that helps families deploy rather than merely commit. Nobody else can make that argument from the inside. Stated carefully: this is not a criticism of the Giving Pledge, which has done enormous good and moved the conversation further than anything before it. It is an observation about what it was never designed to do. 06 Section six · the idea underneath all of it The Signatry means the one who signs Your vision is to write the last check. Israel would boast against me, 'My own strength has saved me.'" — Judges 7:2 Gideon has thirty-two thousand men and an enemy camped in the valley thick as locusts. He is outnumbered before a single sword is drawn, and God's first instruction is not a strategy. It is a reduction. Twenty-two thousand go home before breakfast. Ten thousand remain, and God says it is still too many. By the time the sorting is finished Gideon has three hundred men — ninety-nine percent of his army has walked away — and he is told to attack. Vision without obedience produces talk: grand plans, deferred giving, buildings with a family name on them, a foundation that admires its own balance sheet. Obedience without vision produces faithfulness that never becomes catalytic: a lifetime of good, small, reactive gifts from someone who could have funded a movement and never saw one worth funding. Both engines together produce the people this book is about. They saw something before it existed, and they said yes to a specific assignment inside it before anyone could prove it would work. History remembers the person on the platform. This book is about the one who paid for the platform. That tension is what makes this a book rather than a theme. A Kingdom Funding Prospectus August 2026 01 The Observation The boxes in the garage Ken Sparks handwrote every message he ever preached. Decades of Sundays, box after box of paper, stacked in the order he delivered them. He is not unusual. Walk into the study of almost any pastor who has served twenty-five years or more and you will find some version of those boxes — legal pads, three-ring binders, cassette tapes, aging hard drives, a church website that keeps the last two years online and quietly drops the rest. When he dies, they usually go to the curb within the year — and everything God said through those words goes with them, except what people can still remember. This is a proposal to build the institution that receives it, and to begin with one hundred pastors whose libraries deserve a generation’s care. The people you most need to reach — the owner approaching an exit, the RIA with three hundred relationships, the family already carrying more than it can steward alone — are exactly the people advertising reaches worst. That is not a budget problem. Capacity buys privacy. A family with real means is not persuaded by a claim; they move when a peer speaks or when the professional they already pay hands them something. Every dollar spent buying their attention competes with a referral that costs nothing and carries more weight. So the work is not finding a channel nobody has bought. It is building assets the people who already hold that trust want to pass along — and spending on media only to make those assets findable. Seven ways to build it 1 Make the advisor the channel, not the audience. A large RIA has hundreds of relationships and one recurring problem: how to open a conversation beyond the portfolio. Kingdom Advisors, the custodial conferences, the RIA succession circuit. The instrument is not a booth — it is Steve on a platform and an assessment people leave holding. ST 101 — Syllabus & Course Build Small Group Seminary · Systematic Theology ST 101 What Is Doctrine For? Why theology belongs to the whole church, not just the academy. Sessions 12 Session length 90 min Reading ~140 pp Prerequisite None Tier Foundation Course Description A first course in how doctrine works Most Christians have absorbed a great deal of doctrine without ever being taught how doctrine actually works. They know what their church believes. They are far less sure where those beliefs came from, how they were tested, which of them are worth dividing over, and what any of it has to do with a Tuesday afternoon in a hospital corridor. This course does not attempt to teach the doctrines. That is what the eleven courses after it are for. This one teaches a person how to hold one. It traces the road from a biblical text to a settled teaching, walks through the creeds and confessions that the church has used to guard that road, and gives the student a repeatable method for testing a doctrinal claim. It ends where every course in this program ends, with the student teaching what they have learned to somebody else. Learning Outcomes Explain in plain language what doctrine is, where it comes from, and what it is for. Trace a single teaching from biblical text through theological synthesis to confessional statement. Distinguish first, second, and third order convictions, and explain why that distinction keeps congregations together. Apply a repeatable four-step method for testing whether a doctrinal claim is sound. Describe how doctrine functions pastorally in suffering, in decision-making, in worship, and at a deathbed. Teach one doctrine clearly to another person and receive feedback on it. Texts The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed Provided in the workbook. Read, memorized, and worked through line by line. # A Different Kind of Advisor ## Chapter Seven: The Conversation That Costs You *Draft one. Roughly 3,400 words. Written to be cut.* --- There is a conversation that sits at the center of this work, and almost nobody in our profession has it. I want to describe it precisely, because the vagueness is part of how it survives. A client walks into your office. He is sixty-one. He built a distribution company over twenty-eight years and a private equity group has come at him with a number, and the number is around twenty million dollars. He has never had twenty million dollars. He has had a company worth twenty million dollars, which is an entirely different thing, and he is about to learn how different. He wants to talk about the transaction. What he says is that he needs to think through the tax side. What he means, though he will not say it for another forty minutes and possibly not for another year, is that he is terrified, because the thing he has been for twenty-eight years is about to stop existing, and he does not know what he will be on the other side of it. You know what you should tell him. Some part of you knows it before he finishes his first sentence. You should tell him that if he intends to be generous with any portion of this, the decision has to happen now, before there is a binding agreement, because after that the tax code will treat the gift as though he sold the asset himself and gave away what was left. You should tell him that a gift of company stock before the deal closes is worth roughly twice what the same felt sacrifice is worth after it. You should tell him that the moment to decide what this money is for is now, while it is still theoretical, because in ninety days it will be real and he will be a different man about it. And you should tell him that his children are watching, and that whatever he does in the next six months will teach them more about money than everything he has said to them across their entire lives. # The Deep Well # Chapter One ## The First Thirty Feet The summer I was twelve, Dunmore came up the lane to ask for water, and I watched my father give it to him, and I have thought about that afternoon more than about almost anything else in my life. Dunmore's own supply had gone brackish. He was not a man who asked for things. He stood at the gate with his hat in his hands and did the whole speech he had clearly worked out on the walk over, about how it would only be until autumn and how his boys would come and draw it themselves and not trouble anyone. My father let him get all the way to the end of it. Then he said, "Dunmore. Take what you need." And Dunmore's face did something, and my father put a hand on his shoulder, and there was a moment there that I did not have language for at twelve and would not have language for until I was past forty. Because I was watching two things happen at once and I could only see one of them. The one I saw was generosity, and it was real, and I am not going to take it away from him. The one I did not see was that my father enjoyed it. Not smugly. He was not a smug man. But there was a straightening in him that afternoon, a settling into something, and it came from the fact that the water was his to give and Dunmore's to receive, and that this had been established in front of a boy at a gate on a summer afternoon. Every family has an arrangement like that somewhere, and the people inside it almost never see it, because from the inside it just looks like kindness. --- He called it his well. Not aggressively. He would say I sank that well, or we would not have got through the dry years if I had not put that shaft down, and nobody in the house ever thought twice about it, including me, for about a decade. He had earned the right to say it as far as any of us knew. He had deepened it in his thirties, which was a real piece of work and nearly killed a hired man. # The Deep Well # Chapter Three ## Amos Carried the Water I gave you the short version of Amos once, at a table, with people listening, and the short version made your grandfather sound generous. He was generous. But I told it badly, and I told it in a way that let all of you off, and I am going to tell it properly now because the whole rest of this depends on it. --- Amos came up the lane at a quarter past five, six mornings a week, for twenty-two years. He was a small man with a bad shoulder from something that happened before I was born and that nobody ever explained to me. He carried on a yoke, two vessels, and he made four trips before the household woke and two more in the afternoon, and in the summer he made eight. He had a way of setting a full vessel down on the flags without a sound, which I have tried to do as a grown man and cannot. He knew every one of us by our feet. He would be in the back passage with his back to the door and he would say good morning and my name without turning around, and it was not a trick, it was twenty-two years. Now here is the sentence I want you to sit with, and I am not going to dress it up. I was seventeen years old before it occurred to me that Amos also needed water. Not once. In seventeen years, watching a man carry water into my house every morning of my life, it never entered my head to wonder where he got his own, or how far he walked for it, or who carried it. I did not decide not to wonder. There was no decision. He was part of the architecture of the morning, like the flags in the passage, and you do not ask where the flags go at night. I am telling you that plainly because I want you to notice that I was not a cruel boy. Too little and it is quaint. Water solves that. Everyone needs it, nobody can live without it, and the amount is never the point. # MASTER YOUR MONEY — STUDENT EDITION ### A 6-Part Curriculum & Devotional for Junior High–High School (Built for the Sophomore in the Middle) --- ## How This Version Is Different (and Why) This is a faithful youth adaptation of the adult *Master Your Money* curriculum. The theology is unchanged — **God owns it all, we're stewards in a growth process, faithfulness matters more than the amount, and faith requires action.** What changes is *who's in the room.* A 15-year-old doesn't have a mortgage, a 401(k), or an estate to plan. But they do have a phone, a part-time paycheck or an allowance, a group chat full of comparison, a first debit card, and a brain that is actively deciding *who they are.* That last part is the key: adolescence is the identity-forming season of life, so this version leads with **identity before instructions** — "whose am I" before "what do I do." Every habit we want an adult to have is cheaper, easier, and stickier to build at 16 than at 46. That's the whole pitch. **The seven design moves that make this a best-practice youth curriculum:** 1. **Identity-first, not mechanics-first.** Teens are wired to ask "who am I?" We answer the ownership question *as an identity question*, then let money flow from it. Heart before behavior. 2. **One big idea per session.** Adolescent attention is real and finite. Each session lands a single sticky truth instead of ten sub-points, so students leave able to say it back. 3. **Present-tense, relatable scenarios.** No retirement or estate planning. We use the money life a sophomore actually lives — jobs, phones, comparison, first cards, buy-now-pay-later, gaming purchases, saving for a car. 4. **Timeless principle + timely example, kept separate.** Every session names the eternal truth *and* a disposable modern example, so leaders can swap the example in ten years without the curriculum aging out. 5. **Experiential, not lecture-only.** Each session ends with a *do-it* challenge scaled to a teenager's actual mone

Confidence must be addressed before contentment (you can't settle into "enough" while you're still asking "will I be okay?"). And generosity must precede impact — you have to understand the heart posture before you address strategy. This is consistent with *Generous Living* and Ron Blue's teaching sequence. **Part V (Generosity) is the strongest section** — it distinguishes between different modes of giving (cheerful, proportionate, spontaneous, whole-life) without being redundant.
